Adjacent 9m² (3m × 3m) bed planted with 22 individuals across 14 species. 6 new species added to species_list: Bulbine bulbosa, Dampiera diversifolia, Goodia lotifolia, Lomandra confertifolia 'Little Pal', Olearia ramulosa, Xerochrysum viscosum. 8 top-up plantings of existing species (Kennedia prostrata, Themeda triandra, Leptospermum continentale, Hardenbergia violacea, Brachyscome multifida, Dichelachne crinata, Poa labillardieri, Ozothamnus ferrugineus). Local craft production from natural materials.

Installation commenced today. Underperforming vegetation removed including camellia and buxus. New soil and mulch installed. Habitat rocks placed throughout the garden beds. Micro-topology created across planting zones to guide water movement and create varied conditions for plant establishment. Rocks selected for both aesthetic presence and ecological function -- thermal mass, shelter and soil anchoring.
Two skinks observed in the rock refuge zone shortly after installation. Immediate fauna response to habitat rocks confirms thermal mass and shelter function. Adds to corridor node weighting.

A layered ecological planting designed to create the sense of moving through a small landscape. A stepping-stone path passes through the bed allowing moments of immersion. Taller shrubs and small trees form a woodland backdrop -- Elaeocarpus, Hakea, Leptospermum and Olearia establish the upper layer. Through the middle, grasses including Themeda, Poa and Dichelachne create a flowing matrix, while flowering perennials emerge through to provide cottage seasonal colour. Closer to the path, Myoporum, Dichondra, Pratia and Scaevola soften the ground plane. The bed responds to varying light conditions -- shade-tolerant shrubs behind the path, sun-loving grasses and wildflowers in the open areas.

A sunny, open planting within the lawn as a softer curved island bed. The mature pear remains dominant, with existing silverberry, agapanthus, flax and echium retained to form a light, airy backdrop in grey-blue tones. A crepe myrtle with soft lilac flower is introduced as a new structural tree, tying in with others already in the garden. Through the middle, ornamental grasses and flowering shrubs -- including a large miscanthus as focal point -- give movement and softness. Dianella, carex and euphorbia create repetition and rhythm. Toward the lawn edge, salvias, kniphofia, brachyscome and helichrysum bring seasonal colour while silver-toned and trailing plants soften the boundary between garden and grass. The reduced bed shape improves movement through the space while layered planting suppresses weeds and reduces maintenance.

A sunny, open planting redesigned as a softer curved island within the lawn. The bed has been slightly reduced in size to improve flow and create a stronger sense of openness. The mature pear remains the dominant feature at the northern rear, with the existing silverberry, agapanthus, flax and echium retained to form a light, airy grey-blue backdrop. A crepe myrtle in soft lilac is introduced as a new structural tree to connect this bed to the wider garden. Through the middle, ornamental grasses and flowering shrubs give movement and softness -- a large miscanthus forms a focal point in the lower curve, with dianella, carex and euphorbia creating repetition and rhythm. Toward the lawn edge, salvias, kniphofia, brachyscome and helichrysum bring colour through warmer months while silver-toned trailing plants soften the boundary between garden and grass.

Beth's garden has been designed as a place of calm immersion -- a space where cottage softness meets Japanese-inspired restraint. The canopy of Acer palmatum and dwarf lemon-scented gum creates seasonal presence and dappled light, while sculptural forms like Doryanthes, Hakea and soft drifts of Banksia and Correa anchor the space with structure and habitat value. Beneath this framework, a tapestry of everlastings, billy buttons, flannel flowers and mauve daisies bring pink and purple tones through the seasons, many chosen for their ability to dry beautifully for preserving. The result is a resilient, low-maintenance garden that feels expressive yet grounded -- a place to read, illustrate, forage, hang laundry in the breeze, and quietly lose yourself in beauty year-round.

The front garden has been conceived as a soft meadow arrival -- a gentle, textural landscape with movement and seasonal rhythm. Repurposed bricks are reset into a small meandering path, creating a sense of wander rather than directness, while improving permeability and grounding the space in material honesty. Grasses such as Poa cita provide structure and sway, forming a luminous backdrop for wind flowers, globe thistles and Jerusalem sage. Lavender, catmint and society garlic weave through in mauve and soft purple tones, echoing Beth's love of colour while maintaining resilience. The result is a meadow that feels expressive and romantic but controlled -- a welcoming threshold that shifts beautifully through the seasons.

The Habitat Garden has been designed to bring together native bushland character, wild meadow softness, and selective productive planting. A habitat-rich, low-chemical landscape that supports pollinators, small birds, butterflies, and local insect life while providing a calming daily outlook from the home. The planting palette prioritises Victorian natives, favouring species indigenous to the Surrey Hills area, selected for year-round flowering, seasonal movement, and layered ecological function. This forward-thinking design focuses on long-term resilience, sensory experience and supporting the re-establishment of local biodiversity.

Possums, king parrots, and insects confirmed present. Key gaps identified: absent middle storey, no bird baths, six environmental weeds present. Site analysis completed prior to design. Pre-1770 EVC mapping confirmed Grassy Woodland as the dominant vegetation community. Present-day context shows fragmented remnants -- Valley Grassy Forest in drainage lines, Wattle Park and Surrey Hills Reserve as nearest intact EVCs. Property boundary confirmed via VicPlan -- NRZ3 zone with PPRZ directly adjacent confirming corridor node potential.

Gardener & Son developed a three-zone planting proposal for this Mont Albert property. The Entrance Garden features columnar cherry blossom (Prunus cerasifera 'Oakville Crimson Spire') as a focal tree, underplanted with layered grasses, groundcovers and flowering shrubs including Poa labillardieri, Brachyscome, Lavender and Catmint. The Sensory Garden weaves together aromatic herbs — Rosemary, Curry Plant and Billy Buttons — with native groundcovers Dichondra and Kennedia. The Rear Garden is anchored by Weeping Lilly Pilly (Waterhousia floribunda) with shade-tolerant Aspidistra and Native Violet beneath. Together the three zones deliver five structural layers and 10 indigenous species across approximately 300m² of garden.

All three zones installed. Arborist mulch applied to 75mm depth across planted areas. Garden presented as part of the property's real estate marketing, demonstrating that ecological function and market appeal are not in conflict.
Halictus sp. burrowing bee colony observed in bare soil patch, north corner. First fauna record for the site. Soil patch preserved deliberately.
First 18 species planted across canopy, shrub, grass and groundcover layers. Logs and rocks positioned. Mulch 100mm depth.
180m2 lawn removed following December 2023 heatwave. Soil amended. First mulch layer installed. The question asked: what was here before?

Garden opened to the public through Open Gardens Victoria on 25–26 November 2023. Sam Cox ran garden talks and Q&A at 11am and 2pm both days. Recognised as an exemplar of Australian naturalistic landscape design in private hands. The garden returned to Open Gardens Victoria for a second opening in November 2026.
